\section[o incêndio]{o incêndio — the fire (a large, destructive one)}

\label{lesson:PT-C301-incendio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to damage, then the Portuguese for the harm.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o incêndio}
\textbf{o incêndio} — \textquotedblleft{}the fire (a large, destructive one)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O incêndio destruiu três casas.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The fire destroyed three houses.}
\end{quote}

\emph{O fogo} is any fire; \emph{o incêndio} is one that destroys. \emph{Incêndio florestal} — forest fire.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{incêndio} was borrowed from Latin \emph{incendium} \textquotedblleft{}a conflagration, a fire\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{incendere} \textquotedblleft{}to set on fire\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o incêndio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o incêndio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o incêndio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to damage, then the Portuguese for the harm, then say \emph{o incêndio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o incêndio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The fire (a large, destructive one)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a explosão]{a explosão — the explosion}

\label{lesson:PT-C301-explosao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the harm, then the Portuguese for the fire.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a explosão}
\textbf{a explosão} — \textquotedblleft{}the explosion\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ouvimos uma explosão na fábrica.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We heard an explosion at the factory.}
\end{quote}

Also of feelings: \emph{uma explosão de alegria}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{explosão} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{explōsiō} \textquotedblleft{}a driving off by clapping\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{explōdere}, built on \emph{plaudere} \textquotedblleft{}to clap\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a explosão}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a explosão}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a explosão}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the harm, then the Portuguese for the fire, then say \emph{a explosão} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a explosão mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The explosion\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[explodir]{explodir — to explode, to blow up}

\label{lesson:PT-C301-explodir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the fire, then the Portuguese for the explosion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: explodir}
\textbf{explodir} — \textquotedblleft{}to explode, to blow up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Uma botija de gás explodiu no prédio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A gas bottle exploded in the building.}
\end{quote}

Mostly in the third person: \emph{explodiu, explodem}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{explodir} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{explōdere} \textquotedblleft{}to drive off by clapping, to hiss off the stage\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); the sense of a bang came later.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{explodir}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{explodir}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{explodir}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the fire, then the Portuguese for the explosion, then say \emph{explodir} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does explodir mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To explode, to blow up\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[o extintor]{o extintor — the fire extinguisher}

\label{lesson:PT-C301-extintor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the explosion, then the Portuguese for to explode.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o extintor}
\textbf{o extintor} — \textquotedblleft{}the fire extinguisher\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O empregado apagou o fogo com o extintor.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The employee put out the fire with the extinguisher.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{extinguir}, ‘to put out’.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{extintor} is a learned word from Latin \emph{exstinctor} \textquotedblleft{}one who puts out\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{exstinguere} \textquotedblleft{}to put out, to quench\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the explosion, then the Portuguese for to explode, then say \emph{o extintor} again

\section[a queimadura]{a queimadura — the burn}

\label{lesson:PT-C301-queimadura}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to explode, then the Portuguese for the fire extinguisher.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a queimadura}
\textbf{a queimadura} — \textquotedblleft{}the burn\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele tem uma queimadura na mão.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He has a burn on his hand.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{queimar}. \emph{Queimadura solar} — sunburn.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{queimadura} is built on \emph{queimar} \textquotedblleft{}to burn\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced to Latin \emph{cremāre} \textquotedblleft{}to burn\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), with the ending \emph{-dura}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a queimadura}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to explode, then the Portuguese for the fire extinguisher, then say \emph{a queimadura} again
\end{itemize}
